Why the yield curve matters for your mortgage

8 October

When long-term borrowing costs fall below short-term ones, economists call it an inverted yield curve, and it has preceded most recessions of the past fifty years.

Mortgage rates tend to follow longer-term bond yields rather than the central bank's own rate, which is why fixed deals can get cheaper even before a rate cut.

Lenders price a five-year fix off swap rates, which move with expectations of where interest rates will be over those five years, not where they are today.

That is why brokers say borrowers watching the headline rate alone can be surprised when deals are repriced overnight after a weak jobs report.
